title: Know who you work for (Avot 2:14)
hook: be eager to learn, and know before whom you labor

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Shimon asked that prayer never become keva, a routine. Your line was not rote. What did you say slowly and mean? Today, the last of the five students. Day two hundred sixty-two.

A kid at the dinner table, usually when a guest is there, asks the big one. How do you know God is real? Or, why do we even do this? The adults glance at each other, and somebody says, eat your peas. Today's sage is Rabbi Elazar, usually identified as Elazar ben Arach, the student whose answer won, the one with the good heart. And his saying starts by telling you to be ready for that question.
screen: `THE QUESTION AT THE DINNER TABLE.` → `EAT YOUR PEAS.` → `ELAZAR BEN ARACH.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Elazar says: be eager to learn Torah. Know what to answer an apikoros. And know before whom you toil, and that your employer can be trusted to pay you the wage of your work. Take the strange word first. Apikoros echoes the name Epicurus, a Greek philosopher who taught that the gods take no interest in human affairs. In rabbinic Hebrew, an apikoros is a scoffer, someone who mocks the faith and its teachers. Rabbi Elazar doesn't say avoid them, or shout them down. He says study well enough to answer. Don't be caught with only eat your peas. There's also a quieter way to read it: sometimes the skeptic is the voice inside your own head, at two in the morning. Knowing what to answer means learning enough to face your own questions honestly. Then the second half. Know before whom you toil. All your learning and your work happen in front of someone. There's a related line in the Talmud, sometimes written above the ark in synagogues: know before whom you stand. And then, a picture from the workplace. Your employer is trustworthy, and will pay your wages. The employer, in this saying, is God. In the saying's picture, the work put into learning and living well isn't lost, even when no one else seems to notice. Put together: learn hard, be ready for hard questions, and remember who you're really working for.
screen: `BE EAGER TO LEARN.` · `APIKOROS: FROM EPICURUS.` · `KNOW BEFORE WHOM YOU TOIL.` · `YOUR EMPLOYER WILL PAY.` · then, large: `KNOW WHO YOU WORK FOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: meet one hard question. Settle, and breathe. Let one hard question come up, about faith, or meaning, or why people do what they do. Your own, or one a child or friend has asked you. Don't rush to answer it. Just hold it honestly. Then ask: what's one thing I could learn this week that would help me answer it better? A book, a person to ask, a page of text. The bell holds the time.
Apikoros. A scoffer, a skeptic of the faith: the one Rabbi Elazar says to study hard enough to answer, while remembering before whom you toil.
Your line: know before whom you toil. Today, look up one real answer to a hard question you've been avoiding. Day two hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Jewish learning makes room for hard questions, and the words 'know before whom you stand' appear above the ark in some synagogues as a reminder during prayer.

original.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: know before whom you toil.

trapdoor: what you thought: remember who signs your paycheck.
what it means: study well enough to answer hard questions, and remember your work is done before God.
what a scholar hears: apikoros echoes the name Epicurus, and in rabbinic Hebrew it names a scoffer; one reading says the skeptic to answer is the one inside you.

notes: Avot is paraphrased (outline follows Taylor 1897). The speaker of 2:14 is Rabbi Elazar; most identify him as Elazar ben Arach, the fifth student listed in 2:8, but some editions and commentators read Rabbi Elazar (ben Shamua or another); confirm.
Apikoros from Epicurus is the standard etymology; some rabbinic sources derive it from the Aramaic hefker (lawless). A Keeper may want to note this.
'Know before whom you stand' is Rabbi Eliezer's words to his students in Berakhot 28b; 'many synagogues display it above the ark' is a general claim; confirm.
'The skeptic inside your own head' is attributed loosely to 'later teachers'; confirm or remove.

Editor review: Epicurus did not doubt the gods exist (he taught they are indifferent to humans); 'if they exist' is cut. The Epicurus etymology is now 'echoes the name' in the teach and trapdoor and no longer a myth item or match pair. The Mishnah says only 'Rabbi Elazar', so the hook says 'usually identified as Elazar ben Arach'. Cut 'every kid', 'most of us', 'many synagogues' and the loosely attributed 'later teachers'; the line that the work isn't lost is now framed as the saying's picture, not the narrator's claim.
